Grade 4 · Unit 4.3

Waves, Light, and Information

How do waves, light, and patterns carry energy and information?

Concept 1

Wave patterns have amplitude and wavelength

Waves make repeating patterns, and those patterns can carry energy that moves small objects.

Try it

Rope or rubber-band waves

a rope or rubber band being shaken gently and strongly.

“Make waves in a rope. Some waves are tall. Some waves are close together.”

Diagram

Wave parts

a wavy line labelled amplitude and wavelength.

“Tall waves have big amplitude. Close repeats have short wavelength.”

Try it

Waves move objects

a small cork or paper bit moving on water waves, or rice dancing on plastic wrap near sound.

“A wave can move a cork. Energy travels with the wave.”

Data

Wave observation log

table for small wave and large wave, with object movement.

“Record how far the object moves. Provided dataset: small wave 1 cm; large wave 3 cm.”

Concept 2

Light, reflection, and seeing

We see objects when light reflects from them and enters our eyes.

Diagram

Eye and object

Sun or lamp, apple, eye, arrow from apple to eye.

“Light hits the apple. Some light bounces to your eye.”

Try it

Mirror bounce

flashlight and mirror or shiny foil.

“Aim the mirror. The light changes direction.”

Data

Light-path model

drawing space with source, object, eye, and arrows.

“Draw the path. The arrow into your eye is how you see.”

Real world

Moon

Moon at night.

“The Moon does not make its own light. It reflects sunlight.”

Concept 3

Patterns can transfer information

A pattern of light or sound can carry a message, and we can compare which pattern system works better.

Try it

Signal code

flashlight blinking short and long.

“Short flash, long flash. A pattern can mean something.”

Real world

Traffic light

red, yellow, green lights.

“Color patterns tell drivers what to do.”

Try it

Compare two signals

one team using flashlight code and another using drum or tap code.

“Send the same message two ways. Which one is clearer?”

Data

Signal accuracy table

table with Signal type, Distance, Message correct?

“Record hits and misses. Compare solutions. Provided dataset: flashlight 4 of 5 correct; drum 3 of 5 correct at 5 meters.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Design and compare two signal systems: a flashlight code and a drum/tap code. Teams send the same short message across the room. Criteria: the partner decodes the message correctly at 3 meters. Constraints: no shouting, one pattern key, same distance for both systems. Students record accuracy and choose the better solution with evidence.

Try it

What you need

rope or rubber band, shallow tray, water, small cork or paper bits, flashlight, mirror or shiny foil, paper, tape, cup or small drum, spoon, rice, plastic wrap.

Safety: do not shine lights into eyes; wipe water spills; keep water away from Chromebooks.

Try it

What you do

Make rope waves and water waves. Observe waves moving objects. Model light reflection with mirror and eye-path drawings. Design and compare two signal systems for accuracy.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but the standard expects you to collect your own when you can.

wave movement small wave 1 cm, large wave 3 cm; signal accuracy flashlight 4/5, drum 3/5.

Near you: Great Lakes shipping: lighthouses and fog signals use light and sound patterns. Michigan traffic lights use color patterns to tell drivers what to do.

Words to know

wave
a repeating pattern that can carry energy.
amplitude
wave height; for sound, related to loudness.
wavelength
distance between wave repeats.
reflect
bounce back.
pattern
something that repeats.
signal
a message sent by light, sound, or another code.
information
a message that tells something.
vibration
quick back-and-forth motion.
light
energy we can see.
sound
energy from vibrations.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, standards, pacing

Pacing: five 30-minute sessions.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Waves are only water.” Correct: waves can be in water, in a rope, or in air (sound). Light also moves in a wave pattern, but it does not push a cork the way a water wave does.
  • “Light comes out of our eyes.” Correct: light enters our eyes.
  • “Objects we see make their own light.” Correct: many objects reflect light from another source.
  • “Sound only travels through air.” Correct: sound can travel through solids, liquids, and gases.
  • “Sound can travel through empty space.” Correct: sound needs matter.
  • “Patterns are only decorations.” Correct: patterns can carry information.
  • “Light cannot carry messages.” Correct: light patterns can carry messages.
  • “Waves cannot move objects.” Correct: waves can move small objects by transferring energy.

Limits and cautions:

  • Wave terms are simplified; 4-PS4-1 does not require wave-speed math.
  • Light reflection uses ray models; real scattering is simplified.
  • Sound-moving-rice can be subtle; the provided dataset guarantees evidence.
  • 4-PS4-3 is broad; this unit earns it only if students generate and compare at least two signal solutions with accuracy data.

Michigan Science Standards this unit earns:

  • 4-PS4-1: Develop a model using waves to describe amplitude and wavelength; waves can move objects.
  • 4-PS4-2: Develop a model to describe that light reflects from objects and enters the eye to allow them to be seen.
  • 4-PS4-3: Generate and compare multiple solutions using patterns to transfer information.

Connections: Builds on: Unit 0: How Science Works; 1-A Sound and Light; 4.1 Energy, Speed, and Collisions. Builds toward: Unit 1 Light & Matter; Unit 8.4 Sound Waves; Unit 8.5 Light, Waves & Information.
